topics.name: Mitochondria
topics.kicker: Double-membraned cell organelle · Breaks down food to make usable ATP
topics.dates: Found in nearly every cell in the body
topics.briefing: Mitochondria are bean-shaped organelles nicknamed the “powerhouse of the cell” because they break down digested food to make ATP, the fuel nearly every cell runs on. Folds in their inner membrane, called cristae, pack in extra surface area for this chemical machinery, and each one even carries its own small loop of DNA, passed down only from a person’s mother. Billions of years ago they were likely free-living bacteria that got swallowed by a larger cell and simply stayed.

trap.title: Mitochondria, or chloroplasts?
trap.body: Both organelles have double membranes, both likely began as engulfed bacteria under the endosymbiotic theory, and both carry their own small DNA loop — which is exactly why several real tossups interrupt themselves to say “it’s not the chloroplast, but…” before describing this organelle. The key difference is direction: one breaks food down for energy, the other builds food up from sunlight.
trap.fix: If the clues mention breaking down food, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, or ATP as a final product, it’s mitochondria. If the clues mention capturing sunlight, chlorophyll, or building glucose, it’s chloroplasts instead — never answer “chloroplast” for a mitochondria question.

topics.name: Photosynthesis
topics.kicker: How plants turn sunlight into food · The base of nearly every food chain
topics.dates: Powers nearly every food chain on Earth
topics.briefing: Photosynthesis is how green plants, algae, and some bacteria capture sunlight and turn it into food. Using chlorophyll, often packed inside chloroplasts, they combine carbon dioxide and water into glucose and release oxygen as a byproduct, essentially running in reverse of how animals later burn that same glucose for fuel. The whole process happens in two linked stages: one that needs direct light, and one that uses what the first stage made.

tossups.p: Dutch-British scientist Jan Ingenhousz [“IN-gun-howss”] is usually credited with discovering this process in 1779. In its light-capturing stage, a sequence called the Z-scheme passes electrons donated by a pigment complex named P680.
tossups.r: The sugar-building stage of this process, which happens in the fluid-filled stroma rather than the membrane stacks, is better known as the Calvin cycle. For 10 points, name this process that plants use to turn sunlight into chemical food.

tossups.p: Certain bacteria that perform this process pack a protein shell called a carboxysome around their key enzyme, speeding up this process’s rate. That enzyme, RuBisCo, is considered the most abundant enzyme on Earth.
tossups.r: This process takes in carbon dioxide and water and lets out oxygen as a byproduct. For 10 points, name this process in which plants, algae, and some bacteria build glucose using captured sunlight.

tossups.p: A desert-adapted version of this process, found in plants like cacti, uses crassulacean [“kras-yoo-LAY-shun”] acid metabolism to take in gas only at night. A separate C4 pathway lets some plants run this process efficiently even in hot, dry conditions, unlike the more common C3 version.
tossups.r: This process’s light-capturing stage occurs inside stacked membranes called thylakoids, while its sugar-building stage, the Calvin cycle, happens around them. For 10 points, name this process that converts light into stored chemical food.

tossups.p: This process’s light-capturing stage produces ATP and a related molecule, NADPH, which then power its sugar-building stage. The electron-passing Z-scheme, which runs from a pigment complex called P680 to one called P700, is part of this process’s first stage.
tossups.r: The green pigment chlorophyll absorbs the light that drives this process. For 10 points, name this process that takes place inside a plant’s chloroplasts.

tossups.p: In dry climates, some plants perform a modified version of this process called CAM, opening their pores only at night to limit water loss. A separate C4 pathway is another adaptation that helps certain grasses run this process in hot weather.
tossups.r: Tiny pores called stomata let in the carbon dioxide this process needs, and an enzyme called RuBisCo helps fix that carbon dioxide into sugar. For 10 points, name this process, performed by plants, algae, and oxygen-releasing cyanobacteria, that turns light into food.

tossups.p: Jan Ingenhousz is generally credited with first describing this process in the late 1700s. Certain bacteria boost this process’s efficiency using protein shells called carboxysomes that concentrate carbon dioxide around its main enzyme.
tossups.r: Phloem tissue later carries the sugary product of this process throughout a plant. For 10 points, name this process that uses sunlight to build glucose out of carbon dioxide and water.

tossups.p: This process’s light-capturing stage produces ATP and NADPH, which are then spent during its sugar-building stage to turn carbon dioxide into sugar. That sugar-building stage occurs in the stroma, just outside the thylakoid stacks where light is first captured.
tossups.r: An enzyme called RuBisCo is essential to this process’s carbon-fixing step. For 10 points, name this process that happens inside a plant’s chloroplasts and releases oxygen as a byproduct.

tossups.p: This process’s light-capturing stage begins with a pigment complex called P680 passing along electrons in a sequence known as the Z-scheme. A desert-adapted variant of this process, CAM, only opens its intake pores at night to save water.
tossups.r: The green pigment chlorophyll, and tiny leaf pores called stomata, both play a role in this process. For 10 points, name this two-stage process that converts carbon dioxide and water into glucose using light.

tossups.p: RuBisCo, the enzyme most responsible for this process’s carbon-fixing step, is thought to be the single most abundant enzyme on the planet. Some grasses use an alternate C4 pathway for this process, which is more efficient in hot, bright conditions than the standard C3 pathway.
tossups.r: This process’s sugar-building stage is called the Calvin cycle, and its sugary products later travel through a plant’s phloem. For 10 points, name this light-driven process that builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water.

tossups.p: Bacterial carboxysomes concentrate carbon dioxide to speed up this process’s key enzyme, RuBisCo. This process’s light-capturing stage, which makes ATP and NADPH, takes place inside a chloroplast’s stacked thylakoid membranes.
tossups.r: Most organisms that carry out this process are actually cyanobacteria, which release much of Earth’s oxygen while doing so. For 10 points, name this process, also performed by green plants and algae, that captures light to make food.

tossups.p: Jan Ingenhousz’s 1779 experiments first linked sunlight directly to this process. Its light-driven first stage passes electrons through a sequence called the Z-scheme, running from the pigment complex P680 to P700.
tossups.r: Carbon dioxide enters a leaf through small pores called stomata to supply this process, and the Calvin cycle then turns that carbon dioxide into sugar. For 10 points, name this process that plants use to convert light into chemical food.

tossups.p: A desert-adapted version of this process called CAM, found in plants like cacti, saves water by only opening its pores after dark. This process’s sugar-building stage occurs in the stroma, using ATP and NADPH supplied by the earlier, light-driven stage.
tossups.r: Chlorophyll inside a plant’s chloroplasts absorbs the light that drives this process, and an enzyme called RuBisCo fixes carbon dioxide during its second stage. For 10 points, name this process that releases oxygen as a byproduct.

tossups.r: Phloem transports the sugar this process produces to the rest of a plant, while stomata let in the carbon dioxide this process needs. For 10 points, name this process that turns light into stored chemical food.

tossups.p: This process’s light-driven stage produces both ATP and NADPH, which are then used up converting carbon dioxide into sugar during the Calvin cycle. RuBisCo, the enzyme at the heart of that carbon-fixing step, is often called the most abundant enzyme on Earth.
tossups.r: Chlorophyll absorbs the sunlight that powers this process inside a plant’s chloroplasts. For 10 points, name this process that plants, algae, and cyanobacteria use to make glucose and release oxygen.

trap.title: Photosynthesis, or cellular respiration?
trap.body: These two processes are near-opposites, and middle schoolers often flip them: photosynthesis captures light energy to build glucose (in with carbon dioxide and water, out with glucose and oxygen) inside chloroplasts. Cellular respiration then breaks that glucose back down to release usable energy (in with glucose and oxygen, out with carbon dioxide and water) inside mitochondria.
trap.fix: If the clues mention capturing light, chlorophyll, chloroplasts, or building sugar from carbon dioxide, it’s photosynthesis. If the clues mention breaking down glucose, the Krebs cycle, mitochondria, or releasing energy for the cell to use, it’s cellular respiration instead.

topics.name: Liver
topics.kicker: The body’s detox and metabolism hub · Can regrow itself when damaged
topics.dates: Weighs about 3 pounds in an adult
topics.briefing: The liver is the largest internal organ in the human body, a reddish-brown wedge tucked beneath the right ribs that filters toxins like alcohol straight out of the bloodstream. Its Kupffer cells gobble up worn-out red blood cells, while the greenish fluid it makes, bile, helps the gut digest fat. Heavy drinking can scar it into cirrhosis, but it’s also the only internal organ able to regrow a damaged section.

trap.title: Chromosomes, or just the X?
trap.body: This general answer line accepts specific sex-chromosome guesses like “X chromosome” or “Y chromosome,” since they are just examples. But several real tossups are built entirely around clues that only make sense for one specific chromosome — the X, including Barr bodies, lyonization, fragile X syndrome, or counting a single X (Turner syndrome) versus an extra one (Klinefelter syndrome).
trap.fix: If every clue in the question only makes sense for the X (or another single named one, like 21), give that specific name. If the clues mix in facts true of all of them — a count, karyotypes, mitosis, genes in general — the general answer is safe, and “chromatin” is never correct either way.
trap.line: Real answer line: Chromosomes (accept X/Y/sex/autosomal chromosome; prompt on autosome; do not accept or prompt on chromatin) — a related real tossup instead wants “X chromosome” specifically, and only prompts on bare “chromosome.”
